verses.translation_literal: A song of the ascents. Remember, YHWH, to David, [obj] all his afflictions.
verses.translation_dramatic: A song for the climbing road. The pilgrims lift their voices and begin with a plea: Remember, LORD. Remember David, and every hardship he bore.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the thirteenth of the fifteen Songs of the Ascents (Pss 120–134), the pilgrim songs sung on the way up to Jerusalem. The title is the first line the crowd sings, so play it as walking music, not as a heading read aloud. The psalm then opens with a request that God remember, and in Hebrew thought to remember is to act on what one remembers. The pilgrims are asking God to do something for David's sake, not to recall an old fact.

The KJV's "remember David, and all his afflictions" turns the Hebrew sentence around. The verb takes the preposition לְ "to" or "for": remember, for David, all his afflictions. David is the one who benefits, and the afflictions are the thing God is asked to count in his favour. The KJV also leaves "afflictions" unexplained. The word עֻנּוֹת comes from עָנָה, the root of self-denial and fasting. The commentators read it as the hardship David took on himself while he sought a place for the house, not as suffering done to him: Rashi, Metzudat David and Meiri all take it as David's own toil and anxiety, and the Targum says "mortifications". Radak adds that the psalm is said to belong to the moment David built the altar on Ornan's threshing floor.

"Songs of the ascents" is the plural of מַעֲלָה, "step" or "going up". Whether it names steps of the Temple, the pilgrim climb, or a rising musical pattern is disputed, and the Targum's "ascents of the deep" shows how early the dispute is.

philological_notes.note: Imperative of זָכַר. In covenant language 'to remember' is to act: God remembers Noah, Rachel and Hannah, and then something happens. The plea here is for action on David's behalf.

A noun from עָנָה 'to humble, afflict', with the suffix 'his'. Ibn Ezra takes it as a noun of the same kind as עִנּוּי. Rashi reads it as the self-affliction of David, who laboured to find a place for the sanctuary.

'The ascents', plural of מַעֲלָה 'step, going up'. The heading marks Pss 120–134 as a group of fifteen. The Targum renders it 'ascents of the deep' and Ibn Ezra offers his own occasion for the psalm, and both show that the meaning was open early.

verses.translation_literal: Who swore to YHWH, vowed to the Mighty One of Jacob:
verses.translation_dramatic: He is the one who swore to the LORD, who bound himself by a vow to the Mighty One of Jacob —
verses.directors_commentary:
The relative clause hangs from 'David' in verse 1 and leads straight into the oath itself, so keep the breath unbroken. Swearing and vowing are a parallel pair, the same act said twice for weight (Radak). The KJV's 'How he sware' turns the clause into a narration and adds 'God' in 'the mighty God of Jacob'; Hebrew has only 'the Mighty One of Jacob', an old, archaic epithet of the divine champion also found in Genesis 49:24.

In an ancient Near Eastern setting an oath is a self-curse backed by the deity, so what follows is not a figure of speech: a king is binding his own body to a task. Naming Jacob, the patriarch who himself made a vow about a house of God (Gen 28), places David in the long line of those who vow to God (Radak, Metzudat David).

philological_notes.note: 'The Mighty One of Jacob', an archaic divine title; the noun is a variant of אַבִּיר 'strong, bull'. Metzudat Zion ties it to the sense of strength (Job 24:22); the KJV's 'mighty God' supplies a word that is not there.

verses.translation_literal: If I enter the tent of my house, if I go up onto the couch of my beds,
verses.translation_dramatic: I will not step inside the tent that is my house; I will not climb up onto the couch of my bed —
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a classic oath formula with the curse left unsaid: 'If I do X [may I be cursed]' means 'I will surely not do X'. The KJV 'Surely I will not' captures the sense but erases the shape, and the Hebrew's unfinished 'if' is what makes the oath sound like a man holding his own throat. Metzudat David says exactly this: the 'if' is the language of an oath, left without its ending.

Note the two parallel 'if' clauses, each with a verb of motion toward domestic comfort: entering, and going up. 'Tent of my house' is a stacked phrase; 'tent' survives as a poetic word for a dwelling even after Israel's houses were of stone, and the King's house is the grandest of them. The 'couch of my beds' uses a plural of majesty or intensity for cushions and coverings (Radak: a bed with the fine bedding fit for a king). The KJV's 'tabernacle' is the same word as for the sanctuary tent, so it hides the deliberate irony: David refuses his own 'tent' until God has a place.

philological_notes.note: Used here as the first half of an oath formula: 'if I do this' stands for 'I will not do this', the penalty implied.
'My bedding', plural of a noun from the root for spreading out; the same word is used in Genesis 49:4 of the bed Reuben defiled. Here it marks the royal furnishing of the bed.

verses.translation_literal: If I give sleep to my eyes, to my eyelids slumber,
verses.translation_dramatic: I will not give my eyes their sleep, nor my eyelids so much as a doze —
verses.directors_commentary:
The oath goes on, and the parts of the body are named one by one: eyes, then the eyelids. 'Sleep' and 'slumber' are a pair; the second is the lighter doze (Metzudat Zion calls it 'a light sleep'), so the oath tightens: not even a nap. Radak reads the first as sleep in earnest, Ibn Ezra specifically as the midday sleep; the Hebrew does not decide.

The KJV's 'I will not give' is accurate in sense but loses the grammar of the oath, which is still 'if I give…'. Here the verb is 'give': sleep is something a person hands to himself, so refusing it is an act of will. An ancient king's day ended with rest after labour; to swear off it is to take on the vigil of a watchman. Metzudat David notes the overstatement: the exaggeration of an oath, not a vow of literal sleeplessness.

philological_notes.note: 'Slumber', a light doze, paired with שנת 'sleep' in a poetic sequence that tightens the vow; the same pair stands in Proverbs 6:4.

verses.translation_literal: Until I find a place for YHWH, dwelling places for the Mighty One of Jacob.
verses.translation_dramatic: Not until I have found a place for the LORD — a dwelling for the Mighty One of Jacob.
verses.directors_commentary:
The oath's condition at last, and it is a single word: 'until'. David's vigil has one end, which is to find a place. Note that he says 'find', not 'build': the site has not yet been located (Metzudat David, Rashi: 'until it is known where the sanctuary will be'), and this is the burden of the rest of the poem.

The Hebrew says 'dwelling places' in the plural (מִשְׁכָּנוֹת), where the KJV flattens it to 'an habitation'. Whether this is a plural of majesty, of the sanctuary's several parts (Radak: 'three houses'), or of the tabernacle's many parts is open, and it matters for how the verse sounds: it is a house with many rooms, not a single tent. The same plural comes back in verse 7. 'Place' (מָקוֹם) is the key word of Deuteronomy's 'the place the LORD will choose' (Deut 12), which Malbim cites for this verse.

philological_notes.note: 'Dwelling places', plural of מִשְׁכָּן, the word for the tabernacle. The plural may be of majesty or may count the structure's parts; the KJV's 'habitation' hides the plural.
'Place'; the word has the weight of the 'place the LORD chooses' in Deuteronomy (e.g. Deut 12:5), as Malbim points out.

verses.translation_literal: Behold, we heard of it in Ephrathah; we found it in the fields of Jaar.
verses.translation_dramatic: We heard it whispered in Ephrathah, a rumour passed from mouth to mouth. And now we have found it: out in the fields of Jaar, among the trees.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm switches here from David's vow to the voice of those who went looking. "We" is the company that searched, and the line should feel like a discovery being shared: first a rumour at home, then the thing itself in unfamiliar country. Both verbs have the same feminine suffix, "heard of it", "found it", and the Hebrew gives no noun for what "it" is.

The commentators in our packet read the "it" as the place of the sanctuary, or the Presence that dwells there. Radak takes the feminine to mean the Divine Presence (שכינה) and says the ark's resting place was found where David was answered with fire. A modern reading, not found in the commentators here, takes "it" to be the ark. The noun אֲרוֹן is usually masculine but occasionally feminine, and the previous verses and v. 8 are about the ark's place. Either way, an English reader should know the Hebrew leaves it open.

Ephrathah is the name of David's home district around Bethlehem. Metzudat David says so and cites Genesis 48:7, and Ibn Ezra puts the place near Bethlehem. Rashi offers another reading: Ephrathah as a word for a place of distinction. For the audience it meant home ground, where the old stories of the ark were told. The KJV's "at Ephratah" is fine; the problem is "fields of the wood". יָעַר is a plain Hebrew word for forest, but with no article and in the plural "fields of" it reads as a place name, and the modern identification is Kiriath-jearim, "city of the forests", where the ark stood for twenty years (1 Sam 7:1–2). The commentators say instead that the forest was the grove around Ornan's threshing floor. The Targum has "the fields of the forests of Lebanon, the place where the fathers of the world prayed".

philological_notes.note: The name Ephrathah with the preposition בְּ 'in'. Genesis 48:7 identifies Ephrath with Bethlehem, and Metzudat David links David's birthplace to the verse for that reason.

'Fields of Jaar' or 'fields of the forest'. The English versions all translate it as 'wood' or 'forest'. The modern identification with Kiriath-jearim rests on יָעַר as the second half of that name. The commentators in the packet instead connect the forest to Ornan's threshing floor and to the ram caught in the thicket.
'We heard it', with a feminine suffix. The antecedent is not stated. Rashi glosses the verb as 'the tidings' (הַבְּשׂוֹרָה). A reading of the antecedent as the ark is a modern one.

verses.translation_literal: Let us go in to his dwelling places; let us bow down to the footstool of his feet.
verses.translation_dramatic: Come — let us go into his dwelling, and bow down at the place where his feet rest.
verses.directors_commentary:
The report becomes a summons. These are cohortatives, 'let us…', and in the KJV's 'we will go' they sound like a decision rather than an invitation to the crowd. This is the pilgrim moment: the road ends at the door. 'We will worship' is also soft: the verb is the physical one, 'bow down' (שׁחה), stooping until the body is low.

The 'footstool' is the strong picture. In the ancient Near East a god or king sits enthroned while his feet rest on a stool, and the sanctuary is imagined as that stool: heaven the throne, the temple the place where the divine feet touch earth (Metzudat David; Metzudat Zion: 'the stool placed beneath the feet of a person sitting'; Radak: it lines up with the throne of glory above). The plural 'dwelling places' returns from verse 5.

philological_notes.note: 'The footstool of his feet': the sanctuary as the stool under the enthroned God's feet. Metzudat David explains it as a figure in which his seat is in heaven and his feet come down to rest in the temple.
'Let us bow down', a bodily act of prostration, wider than the KJV's 'worship'.

verses.translation_literal: Arise, YHWH, to your resting place, you and the ark of your strength.
verses.translation_dramatic: Rise, LORD, and come to your rest — you, and the ark that is your strength.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the song turns from the people to the God they have been addressing in the third person. The cry 'Arise, YHWH!' is the old formula spoken when the ark set out on the march (Num 10:35), and now it is spoken for the last journey. The KJV's 'into thy rest' is fine in sense, but the Hebrew word, מְנוּחָה, is a place of settled rest after wandering, the opposite of the tent-to-tent travelling that Metzudat David and Meiri describe.

The pairing 'you and the ark' is striking: God and his ark are named together, as two things that move in step. 'The ark of your strength' is not 'the mighty ark' but the ark that is the seat of God's strength (Metzudat David points to its power against the Philistines in 1 Samuel). Radak and Malbim note that Solomon speaks these lines again at the dedication of the temple (2 Chr 6:41), so an audience in the temple would hear it as a liturgical echo.

philological_notes.note: 'Resting place', a settled seat after wandering; used for the place where the LORD would settle for good.
'The ark of your strength', the ark as the sign of God's might; Metzudat David links it to the ark's deeds among the Philistines.

verses.translation_literal: Your priests, let them put on righteousness, and your faithful ones, let them ring out.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let your priests be robed in righteousness, and let your faithful ones lift their voices and ring out their joy.
verses.directors_commentary:
The prayer to the LORD for his resting place now turns to the people who will serve there, and it asks for two things: the priests dressed, and the faithful singing. Priests in the ancient world were identified by what they wore, and the verb לָבַשׁ "to put on" is the ordinary one for clothing. The line says "let them put on righteousness", as if righteousness were a garment. Metzudat David and Radak both take the garments of the priesthood to be the "garments of righteousness", and Malbim adds that the clothing pictured the moral qualities the soul should wear. The KJV's "clothed with righteousness" keeps that image and so is accurate.

The second half uses רָנַן, a ringing public cry, the sound of a crowd in a procession, not a private feeling. The KJV's "shout for joy" and YLT's "cry aloud" both have it. חֲסִידֶיךָ is the plural of חָסִיד, one who keeps חֶסֶד, covenant loyalty. The KJV's "saints" is an archaism: these are not holy persons set apart but faithful members of the covenant community. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri identify them with the Levites, the singers of the sanctuary, and Meiri cites Deuteronomy 33:8, "your faithful one" said of Levi. The Targum agrees, with "Levites".

philological_notes.note: 'Let them put on righteousness': the garment image. The commentators read it of the priestly vestments, which Metzudat David says atone and justify sinners.
From חָסִיד, 'one who practises חֶסֶד', covenant loyalty. The KJV's 'saints' reads as a holy elite. Ibn Ezra and Meiri take it to mean the Levite singers.
Piel of רָנַן, 'to ring out, cry aloud'. It is the sound of a public celebration.

verses.translation_literal: For the sake of David your servant, do not turn back the face of your anointed one.
verses.translation_dramatic: For David's sake, your servant — do not turn away the face of the one you anointed.
verses.directors_commentary:
The plea is made on David's account, not on the speaker's merit: 'for the sake of' is the language of a favour owed to a loyal servant. The KJV's 'turn not away the face' is literal and correct, but modern ears take it as a vague snub. The phrase means to send a petitioner back empty-handed: to 'turn back the face' of someone who has come to ask (Metzudat David: do not send his face back empty).

He is the LORD's 'servant', and also 'anointed', a priestly and royal word (משיח) for one set apart by oil. The two titles together are the king's two claims on God: service rendered, and office conferred. Rashi connects the line to Solomon bringing the ark into the temple; Ibn Ezra reads 'anointed' as David himself, since the doubled line explains the 'for the sake of' clause. The text does not say. Ancient listeners would hear the plea with whichever king was before them.

philological_notes.note: 'For the sake of'. STEPBible's 'forsake of' is a mistake; the word is a preposition from עבר 'to pass over', meaning on account of.
'Do not turn back the face of': to refuse a petitioner, sending him away unheard.
'Your anointed one'. Rashi reads it as Solomon at the ark's entry, Ibn Ezra as David; the form does not decide.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH swore to David [in] truth; he will not turn back from it: From the fruit of your belly I will set [one] on a throne for you.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD swore to David, and he swore it true, an oath he will not take back: One from the fruit of your own body I will set upon your throne.
verses.directors_commentary:
The mood turns here from petition to answer. After the pilgrims' prayer, in v. 10, that God not turn back (תָּשֵׁב) the face of his anointed, the psalm recalls an oath that God himself will not turn back from (לֹא יָשׁוּב). It is the same root שוב, "to turn", and in both verses God is the one who might turn. In v. 10 he is asked not to turn the anointed away. In v. 11 he is said never to turn away from his own oath. The prayer rests on the promise: God has already bound himself, so the plea is not for something new.

The oath is the promise of 2 Samuel 7 as the commentators read it (Radak and Metzudat David both cite Nathan's message). A promise from the LORD was an oath, because a promise made by God is as binding as an oath sworn by a person. The KJV's "in truth" for אֱמֶת is fine, though the word means reliability as well as accuracy, which YLT's "truth" keeps.

Two things in the KJV are worth watching. "Fruit of thy body" is the polite rendering of פְּרִי בִטְנְךָ, literally "the fruit of your belly", and the Hebrew points at the child as something that came out of David's own body, with all the physicality that has. And the KJV's "will I set upon thy throne" fills in an object the Hebrew leaves unstated: there is no noun after "I will set", only "from the fruit of your belly", and the throne is "for you", David's own.

philological_notes.note: 'He will not turn back', with God as the subject. It echoes the hiphil תָּשֵׁב of v. 10, where God is asked not to turn back the anointed's face; here God himself will not turn back from his oath.
'Fruit of your belly': a descendant, literally one who came from David's own body. Radak ties it to the promise in 2 Samuel 7 and its 'who shall come out of your bowels'.

verses.translation_literal: If your sons keep my covenant and my testimonies, this [which] I will teach them, also their sons, until perpetuity, will sit on a throne for you.
verses.translation_dramatic: If your sons keep my covenant, and the testimonies I will teach them, then their sons also, to the end of time, shall sit upon your throne.
verses.directors_commentary:
The unconditional-sounding oath of verse 11 now carries its condition: 'if'. The promise to David's person is firm, but the passage down through the generations rests on the sons keeping the covenant (Malbim: a condition for the sons' sons). This is the verse that sets the stakes for every king that follows; it is the sword hung over the whole dynasty.

The KJV 'children' flattens בנים, which is 'sons', the male heirs in line for the throne. 'Testimony' (עדות) is the covenant's witness-document, the commands as a legal record. The odd 'zo' ('this, which') is a rare relative; Rashi explains it as 'that which I will teach them', and the verb 'teach' is imperfect: God promises to go on instructing, through prophets (Radak, Metzudat David). The KJV 'for evermore' renders a doubled phrase, עֲדֵי־עַד, 'unto perpetuity'. The chain 'sons, then their sons' is the dynasty seen in the long view, not one generation.

philological_notes.note: 'My testimonies'; the pointing with holem for shureq is irregular, and the commentators treat it as a form of עדות, the covenant's witness.
A rare relative, 'which, that'; Rashi glosses 'that which I will teach them'.
'Until perpetuity', a doubled expression for the longest reach of time; the KJV's 'for evermore' is the usual rendering.

verses.translation_literal: For YHWH has chosen Zion; he has desired it for a dwelling-place for himself.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the LORD himself has chosen Zion. He has longed for her, and he has wanted her as the place where he will dwell.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the hinge of the psalm. Up to verse 12 the voice has been David's oath and the LORD's oath in answer; here the choir turns from the king to the place, and the reason for the house of David is given: the LORD chose Zion first. The kî, 'for', ties the promise of the dynasty to the choice of the city, and the Malbim reads the order just so: the choice of David's line rests on the choice of Zion.

Play the verb בָּחַר as a deliberate act of will, a selection made out of many places, and the next verb as something warmer. אִוָּה is the language of craving and longing, not of administrative designation. The same root is used for a person's appetite (Deut 12:20) and for the soul's desire (Job 23:13, which Metzudat Zion cites for this verse), so the LORD is pictured as wanting this hill the way a person wants a home. The KJV's 'he hath desired it' is faithful, and 'habitation' is a fair rendering of מוֹשָׁב, though the word is plainer than it sounds: a seat, a place where one sits down to stay. Ibn Ezra notes that Zion is named here because it was called the city of David.

For an audience that remembered the ark moving from tent to tent, this is the end of wandering. The Radak and Meiri both hear it that way, as the LORD no longer going from place to place or from tent to tent. The final לוֹ, 'for himself', is easy to lose: the dwelling is for the LORD's own sake, not for the king's.

philological_notes.note: To choose, select. It takes its object with the preposition בְּ, as here: 'chose Zion', not 'chose in Zion'. The verb stresses a deliberate pick among alternatives, which is how the Malbim reads it ('on the side of choice against the other places').
He has desired it: a perfect verb with a feminine suffix, referring to Zion. The root is that of craving and longing, warmer than 'choose'. Metzudat Zion glosses it as desire and compares Job 23:13.
A seat, a place of settled sitting or dwelling, from 'to sit, to dwell'. It implies a permanent residence in contrast with the movement of the tent.

verses.translation_literal: This [is] my resting-place for ever and ever; here I will sit, for I have desired it.
verses.translation_dramatic: This is my rest, now and for all time to come. Here I will sit down and stay, for I have wanted this place, and I want it still.
verses.directors_commentary:
The voice is now God's own. This answers the plea of verse 8, 'Arise, O LORD, to your resting-place', and the word is the same, m'nuchah: not a pause on a journey but the end of one. The ark had travelled from Shiloh to captivity, to a stranger's house, to a tent; for a people who had seen it carried about, 'here' (poh) is the sharpest word in the line. A pointing, almost a finger laid on the ground.

The KJV 'for ever' flattens the doubled expression 'adei-'ad, literally 'until perpetuity', 'to the end of the end'. Its 'I will dwell' is acceptable, but the verb is yashav, 'sit', the posture of a king enthroned and at ease. The closing 'for I have desired it' is the reason and repeats the verb of verse 13 in the first person, so the verse ends with God saying aloud what the narrator had only reported.

philological_notes.note: 'My resting-place', the settled rest that follows wandering. Malbim reads the verse as the reply to 'Arise, O LORD, to your resting-place' and stresses that God does not rest here only because he is weary of moving, but for the place's own sake.
'Until perpetuity': a construct form followed by the absolute, an emphatic way of saying 'for ever'.

verses.translation_literal: Her provision I will bless, bless; her needy ones I will satisfy [with] bread.
verses.translation_dramatic: Her harvests I will bless, and bless again. Her poor, who go hungry elsewhere, I will fill with bread until they want no more.
verses.directors_commentary:
God now speaks the blessings that answer the prayers of the psalm's first half, and he starts with food. In an agrarian economy, with one rain-fed harvest a year and famine only one failed season away, the promise to 'satisfy with bread' is the most concrete form of salvation there is. And it is the poor, the evyonim, who are named, the people who could not buy their way through a bad year.

The KJV 'abundantly bless' is fair as sense but hides the grammar: Hebrew puts the infinitive and the finite verb side by side, barekh avarekh, 'blessing I will bless', and the repetition is the abundance. 'Her provision' (tzeidah) is a rare word, and the traditional commentators take it as food for the road or the land's yield (Meiri). Say it as a promise with an open hand.

philological_notes.note: 'Her provision, her food', from the word for what is hunted or gathered for a journey, hence supplies. Meiri explains it as 'her food, as in provision for the road'; Rashi glosses it simply as 'her sustenance'.
An infinitive absolute before a finite verb of the same root: 'blessing, I will bless', for emphasis and certainty.
'Her needy ones', those in want. Radak: even the poorest in her will be filled with bread.

verses.translation_literal: And her priests I will clothe [with] salvation, and her faithful ones, shout for joy, they will shout for joy.
verses.translation_dramatic: And her priests I will robe in rescue. And her faithful will sing, and sing out, sing until the courts ring with it.
verses.directors_commentary:
This verse is a deliberate mirror. In verse 9 the people prayed, 'Let your priests be clothed with righteousness, and let your faithful shout for joy.' God now answers each half and raises it: where they asked for righteousness, he gives yesha, 'salvation' or deliverance; where they asked for joy, he doubles it. Malbim sees exactly this answer to the earlier prayer.

The image is of clothing because priests were defined by their garments, the linen and the turban of the sanctuary. Radak says: they wear my garments in my service, and I will wear them in my salvation. The KJV 'I will also clothe' adds an 'also' that is not there, and 'saints' sounds like a later, churchly word; chasidim are the loyal, those who keep covenant faithfulness (chesed). Ibn Ezra and Radak take them as the Levites, the singers. Again the Hebrew pairs the infinitive with the finite verb, 'ranen yeranenu': joy that cannot be said once.

philological_notes.note: 'Her faithful ones', people marked by chesed, loyal love. Ibn Ezra and Radak take them as the Levites who sing in the sanctuary; Radak notes that Moses called Levi 'your faithful one'.
A shout of joy, a ringing cry, in the intensive form with an infinitive absolute: 'shouting, they will shout'. It is the answer to verse 9's single 'let them shout'.

verses.translation_literal: There I will make a horn sprout for David; I have arranged a lamp for my anointed.
verses.translation_dramatic: There, in that very place, I will make a horn grow for David, strong and rising. I have set the lamp in order for my anointed, and it will not go out.
verses.directors_commentary:
'There' (sham) is the hinge: in Zion, where God has chosen to sit, the dynasty will flower. And the verb is botanical. A horn is the animal's weapon and the sign of strength and rank, so a horn that sprouts (atzmiach) is a mixed image on purpose: power that grows like a shoot out of a stump. Radak notes that 'I will make it sprout' implies that it had withered first.

The KJV 'I have ordained a lamp' is far from the verb: arakhti is the word used for arranging, laying out in rows, as the priest arranges the lamps and the show-bread. God is the one who trims and sets the lamp. A lamp is a dynasty that keeps burning: elsewhere a king's line is called David's lamp (1 Kings 11:36). The KJV also loses 'my anointed' as a person: mashiach is a king, anointed with oil, not yet the capitalized title of later readers. Play it as quiet certainty, a lamp being lit in a dark room.

philological_notes.note: 'I will make a horn sprout.' The horn is a standard image of strength and status; Metzudat Zion says the word is borrowed for rule and power because horned animals gain strength in fighting. The verb is that of plants, so power is pictured as growth.

'I have arranged, set in order', the verb of laying out things in their proper rows. Metzudat Zion: 'a matter of arrangement'; Ibn Ezra compares 'Aaron and his sons shall arrange it' (Exod 27:21) for the lamps of the sanctuary.
A lamp. Radak: the king is like a lamp that gives light to the people.

verses.translation_literal: His enemies I will clothe [with] shame, and on him his diadem will blossom.
verses.translation_dramatic: His enemies I will dress in shame, wrapped in it from head to foot. But on him, on David's own head, the crown will break into bloom and shine.
verses.directors_commentary:
The garment image from verse 16 returns for the last time, and it divides two groups. The priests are clothed with salvation; the enemies are clothed with boshet, shame. Metzudat David notes that the clothing wraps the whole body, so there is no part of them left uncovered. In a culture of honour and shame, being 'dressed' in shame is public exposure, the reverse of rank.

The last line is a pun waiting to be heard. The verb yatzitz means to blossom or flower, and it is also the root of the word for the gold plate on the high priest's turban, the tzitz (Exod 28:36), which Radak mentions as one reading. The nezer, the diadem, is itself a word of consecration, the 'separating' sign of the king. So the crown does not merely shine: it flowers, the very image of the horn that sprouted in verse 17. The KJV 'upon himself shall his crown flourish' is accurate in sense, though 'flourish' is a growing word that hides the 'sparkle' that Rashi proposes. Say it with a lifting, brightening voice, after the heavy shame of the first line.

philological_notes.note: 'It will blossom, bloom', and by extension shine. Rashi takes it as 'shine' (compare Ezekiel 1:7, 'sparkling'); Ibn Ezra as 'go out and be seen'. The same root gives the tzitz, the gold plate of the high priest's turban, in a reading Radak records.
His diadem, the sign of consecration worn by a king or high priest. Metzudat Zion glosses it simply 'his crown'.
Shame, public disgrace; here a garment put on by the enemy, mirroring the 'salvation' put on by the priests in verse 16.
